bio.en: Gokul Rajaram is a product and business leader at DoorDash, a prolific angel investor, and a board member at companies including Coinbase, Pinterest, and The Trade Desk, who describes himself simply as a 'startup helper.'
bio.zh: Gokul Rajaram 是 DoorDash 的产品与业务负责人、高产的天使投资人，并担任 Coinbase、Pinterest、The Trade Desk 等公司的董事，他却把自己简单称作一名“创业帮手”。

summary.en: Gokul packs in practical wisdom on choosing where to work, how to do product development at startups, structuring product teams, hiring, and angel investing—all while balancing an intense DoorDash job, multiple public-company boards, and a busy mentoring schedule. He's known as one of the most humble, generous operators in tech, and the episode is a wide-ranging tour of lessons from someone who helps founders constantly. Listeners get concrete guidance on the decisions that most shape a builder's career.
summary.zh: Gokul 浓缩了大量实用智慧：如何选择工作平台、如何在创业公司做产品开发、如何组织产品团队、如何招聘以及如何做天使投资——而这一切都要在 DoorDash 高强度工作、多家上市公司董事身份和繁忙的导师日程之间取得平衡。他以科技圈最低调、最慷慨的操盘手之一而闻名，这期节目是一场地地道道的“过来人”经验巡礼。听众能收获关于那些最能塑造建设者职业生涯的决策的具指导。

turns.speaker: Gokul Rajaram
turns.en: Thank you Lenny. It's awesome to be here. Thanks for having me.
turns.zh: 谢谢你，Lenny。很高兴能来参加节目。感谢邀请。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's absolutely my pleasure. You're on the boards of Coinbase and Pinterest, you're a really big deal at DoorDash. You're even bigger deal at Caviar. You worked at Square, at Facebook, at Google. Plus you're an incredibly prolific investor. I'd probably put you in the top 1% of investors based on what I've seen. And so I'm just curious kind of just to set context, how did you get into tech and product originally? And then just what was your journey like to becoming this luminary of tech?
turns.zh: 真是荣幸之至。您同时是Coinbase和Pinterest的董事会成员，在DoorDash的地位举足轻重，在Caviar更是备受瞩目。您曾任职于Square、Facebook和谷歌等公司，更是一位极其活跃的投资者。以我所见，您绝对能跻身全球顶尖1%的投资者之列。所以我很好奇，您最初是如何踏入科技与产品领域的？又经历了怎样的历程，才成为当今科技界的领军人物？

turns.speaker: Gokul Rajaram
turns.en: First of all, let's not start use the word luminary. I think it's people like Elon and Mark who are luminaries, I think. I've just been lucky to work at good companies and observe the creation and growth of these companies. I'll give you an interesting story. Crazily enough, I joined Google as a PM after I applied to Cisco. This was in 2003, and I wanted to be a hardcore networking product manager in the layer three, layer two of networking. I was like, layer seven software is for wimps. I'm going to go hardcore. (00:03:50): Cisco had a... In 2001, 2002 right after the bust, the first dot com bust. Then Cisco actually rescinded my offer. They made me an offer, they rescinded it, and then basically that's how I ended up at Google. Was my second choice after Cisco. So literally you can see some of these decisions. You're just saved from yourself by [inaudible 00:04:08], and otherwise I would have been in networking, probably. Maybe still at Cisco. But at Google I got put on something called syndication, which is taking Google searches results and ads and then syndicating it to other properties like AOL back in the day, Yahoo, et cetera. (00:04:21): And I was working on that product and at about 6:00 PM... We had offices then, back then at Google, 2002, 2003, people would go home and some people would stay back. I'd just walk around and a few doors from me, I basically found a group of engineers in an office and they were working on something. I was like, "What are you working on? They said, "Well," Serge Brin, the co-founder had given them a project of essentially reversing what Google had done with search. You type in a phrase, set of keywords and then Google identifies the webpages that are most relevant to the set of keywords. So we have an index that matches keywords and webpages, so why don't we extract those keywords for any given webpage and basically see if we can target ads based on that? So that seemed interesting. Google's AdWords product, which was such, ads had just started scaling up and I was like, "Hey, do you have any PMs working with you?" (00:05:09): They said, no. "Can I be your PM?" They said, "Aren't you working on syndication?" I said, "Yeah, but I can do this nights and weekends." So I basically became a part-time PM for them and help them talk to customers, even did presentations with them. And while my full-time job was this other thing. And essentially within three months this thing grew big enough and fast enough and became a product that my boss saw this and she moved me over to full-time work on this, and that became Google AdSense. So a lesson for me I realized is that it's very important to do a core job really well at any company, but it's equally important to have curiosity and be open to serendipity. I think Zoom makes it harder, but it's very important to understand what else is going on at the company, what else people are working on, and just keep talking to people and build relationship with the company, because those are what will lead to the next set of opportunities. (00:05:57): I think many opportunities don't come linearly just working in your job and making sure you get promoted. That's not how I think great careers are built. I think great careers are built by knowing a lot of people doing great work so they know and want you on their teams, and just waiting for serendipity and then seizing it and jumping. Another example is I had advised a company which was acquired by Square, and the fundraiser in Google. And Jack, the CEO of Square, asked the founder who was one of the best product people he knows. My name was mentioned. So then they reached out to me and I would never have really... I mean, informal advising. I didn't have any equity of something in the company. I just helped them out because they reached out to me because it was a former colleague and I said, "Sure, I'll help you out." (00:06:38): And then that resulted in him saying good things about me and that led to the inbound from Square. So I think you got to prioritize this stuff. I mean you got to be careful it doesn't take up your life, but I think it's very important to be curious and open to serendipity. I realize in today's world there are lots of crazy serendipity things that happen. If you take inbounds from smart people and you just chat with them and you help them out. (00:06:58): Paying it forward is the other thing, paying it forward. Lenny, you're a great example to this, you pay it forward so much. Your articles, stuff you write, good things happen in ways that you don't even realize. You build up a reservoir of goodwill that comes back to help you in different ways.
turns.zh:
首先，咱们先别急着用“杰出人物”这个词。我觉得像埃隆（Elon）和马克（Mark）这样的人才才是真正的“杰出人物”。我只是幸运地在优秀的公司工作过，见证了这些公司的诞生与成长。让我分享一个趣事。说来奇怪，我2003年申请思科（Cisco）后，最后却去了谷歌（Google）担任产品经理。当时我想成为一名专攻三层、二层网络产品的硬核产品经理，觉得层七软件太不靠谱了，自己要走硬核路线。

（00:03:50）：说回思科。2001年、2002年，刚经历过互联网泡沫破裂，思科在第一轮泡沫后果断撤回了我的录用通知。他们先是给了我录用函，又撤回了，最终我才转投谷歌。这其实是我在思科之后的第二选择。可见人生有时会被意外打断，而你往往会从中受益。

（00:04:21）：在谷歌2002至2003年间，我负责一个名为"联合发布"（syndication）的项目，负责将谷歌的搜索结果和广告推送到其他平台，比如AOL、雅虎等。当时快下班时，我路过邻近办公室，发现几位工程师正在开发一个项目。他们说创始人谢尔盖·布林（Serge Brin）给他们布置的任务，是反向应用谷歌的搜索算法：用户输入关键词，系统会匹配最相关网页。既然能精准匹配关键词和网页，为何不反向提取网页中的关键词，再基于这些关键词投放广告？这个想法让我兴奋不已。当时谷歌的AdWords广告业务刚刚起步，我问他们是否需要PM，他们说不需要。我反问：“我能当你们的PM吗？”他们说：“你不是在做联合发布吗？”我回答：“没错，但我可以利用晚上和周末时间兼职。”于是我成为兼职PM，协助他们对接客户，甚至参与演示。而我的全职工作仍在其他部门。三个月内，这个项目迅速壮大，成为产品，老板随即将我转为全职，成就了AdSense。由此我领悟到：在任何公司，做好核心工作至关重要，但保持好奇心、拥抱机遇同样重要。远程办公让这变得更难，但更要了解公司动态、关注同事项目、持续社交，这才是抓住下一个机遇的关键。

（00:05:57）：我认为许多机会并非循规蹈矩地通过晋升获得的。我不认同这种职业发展观。伟大的职业生涯源于结识众多优秀人才，让他们认可你并渴望你加入团队，然后等待机遇来临，果断行动。另一个例子是，我曾为一家被Square收购的公司提供咨询服务，Square的CEO杰克（Jack）后来在谷歌募资。杰克向创始人询问是否需要PM，创始人推荐了我——这位创始人曾是我在谷歌最敬佩的产品经理之一。
他认识的一些人。我的名字被提及了。于是他们联系了我，而我绝不会真的……我是说，非正式的建议。我在那家公司没有任何股权。我只是帮了他们一把，因为他们联系了我——毕竟是前同事——我当时就说，“好的，我会帮你的。” （00:06:38）结果他对我的评价很好，然后Square就主动联系了我。所以我觉得你得优先处理这些事情。我是说，你得小心别让它们占据你的生活，但我认为保持好奇心和对机缘巧合持开放态度非常重要。我意识到在当今世界，许多疯狂的机缘巧合都会发生。如果你接受聪明人的邀请，跟他们聊聊天，帮他们一把，（00:06:58）这就是传递善意的另一种方式。莱尼，你就是一个很好的例子，你经常传递善意。你写的文章、分享的见解，善意的种子总会以你意想不到的方式回馈给你。你积累的善意储备，最终会以各种方式助你一臂之力。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love this advice. I don't know if you know this already, but I actually did a TEDx talk once about serendipity. It's called Losing Your Serendipity. It's out there on the internet, in case people want to-
turns.zh: 我太爱这条建议了。不知道你是否了解，我曾经做过一场TEDx演讲，主题是"失去意外之喜"。演讲视频在网上可以找到，感兴趣的朋友可以去看看。

turns.speaker: Gokul Rajaram
turns.en: I'm going to check it out. Wow.
turns.zh: 我得去看看。哇哦。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Long time ago. But I love, love that concept and it's such a good story. Just kind of pulling that thread a little bit, I'm curious, when you're looking for opportunities, would you suggest people focus on things they're excited about and passion that's pulling them in? (00:07:36): Or more, I just think there's a big opportunity and maybe I'm not so excited about doing the work, but I'm just going to follow it because it may lead somewhere. Or some, right in the middle? How do you think about that?
turns.zh: 那已经是很久以前的事了。但我真的超爱这个概念，这背后还有个很棒的故事。顺便说一句，我很好奇，当人们寻找机会时，你会建议他们专注于自己热爱且充满激情、深深吸引他们的事物吗？（00:07:36）或者更具体地说，我可能对某项工作没那么兴奋，但还是会坚持下去，因为它或许会带来转机。又或者介于两者之间？你怎么看？

turns.speaker: Gokul Rajaram
turns.en: I think you got to think about the day to day. In many cases I feel people don't realize whether they're passionate about something or not until they actually start doing the work. I could never ever imagine that I could be passionate about payments ever in a million years, but the environment of the company Square was so infectious and great and the culture was so good that we even made working on payments... And you're serving these small businesses. I always think of, not what you're working on but what problem you're solving. In many cases, I get more energy from the problem I'm solving and who I'm solving it for and I realize that I get much more energy from personally solving problems that affected a small business or basically people or small business that I can relate to. It is harder for me to get energy solving problems of big enterprise and companies. (00:08:28): So I've always somehow ended up working at companies like DoorDash or Square or even Facebook, building ad product for small businesses, Google AdSense for small publishers. And so consumers for small businesses is what I've seen. And so I think it's important to know what kind of problems you get energy from and really think about the problem versus the customer segment. Maybe even more than the problem because I've saw different kinds of problems, but I realize that it's those kinds of customers I enjoy because you can meet them in the day to day. You can see them on the street or you read their articles. A small blogger for example, I remember I used to go to a lot of blog conferences when I was a PM for AdSense. It was great to meet these bloggers. They would be hundreds of thousands of them back then. (00:09:10): It's probably different, Medium and so on, now, Substack, but back then it was blogger. I think the word doesn't even exist today, but it's amazing to meet them and they literally... Till today I have people emailing me, "Gokul, I know you right? We used to make a hundred thousand dollars a year based on purely AdSense, and that was our living and that's how we built this other company on that." So big companies, you don't ever get to hear something like that. So I got energy from things like that. The other one is founder. I think, Lenny, it's very important if you think... Talking about company, is to have a founder, when you talk to them, you don't get the sense that they're in it for the money. I think it's very important for founders to really live and breathe the mission themselves in an authentic way. (00:09:48): And if people are smart, and I think you've got to really honestly think if this person is constantly talking about revenue and trying to convince you that you're going to get wealthy or they're going to get... Whatever the case is, that's not the kind of founder that's going build a really large company. And so if you look at everyone, whether it's... You've worked with Brian Chesky, I'm sure he embodies that. Jack at Square, Tony at DoorDash, Larry at Google, all of these folks embody that mission. Mark at Facebook. That they care about winning. They will win and money will come, but it's a side product. It's not the main thing they're aiming for.
turns.zh:
我觉得你得从日常工作中去思考。在很多情况下，我发现人们直到真正开始做这份工作后，才会意识到自己是否对某件事充满热情。我永远也想不到自己会对支付行业产生兴趣，但Square公司的环境太有感染力了，文化也非常棒，以至于我们甚至能把做支付的工作变得充满乐趣……而你们服务的对象是小企业。我总是思考的不是你在做什么工作，而是你在解决什么问题。很多时候，我从所解决的问题中获得更多能量，从为谁解决问题中获得灵感。我发现，为小企业或与我息息相关的人们解决问题时，个人成就感最强。而解决大企业的难题则更难激发我的热情。  
（00:08:28）所以我最终总是选择像DoorDash、Square甚至Facebook这样的公司，为小企业开发广告产品，为小型出版商开发Google AdSense。消费者群体是小企业，这才是我看到的现实。因此，了解自己从哪些问题中获得能量，真正思考问题而非客户群体，可能更为重要。甚至比问题本身更重要，因为我接触过各种各样的问题，但最终发现真正让我享受的是与这些客户的互动——你能在日常生活中遇到他们。在街上看到他们，或是读到他们的文章。比如一位小博主，我记得在AdSense担任产品经理时，经常参加博客大会。能与数十万博主交流真是太棒了。（00:09:10）现在可能不同了，比如Medium、Substack之类的，但那时还是以博客为主。如今这个词甚至可能不常用了，但能与他们交流真是令人惊叹。他们真的……直到今天还有人给我发邮件说：“Gokul，我认识你吧？我们当年仅靠AdSense每年就能赚10万美元，那就是我们的生计，靠这个我们创办了另一家公司。”大公司可没人会跟你分享这样的故事。正因如此，我从这类事中获得能量。另一个例子是创始人。我觉得，Lenny，如果你考虑公司的话，有一个创始人很重要。当你与他们交流时，能感觉到他们不是为了钱而做事。我认为创始人真正以真诚的方式践行使命至关重要。（00:09:48）聪明的人会仔细观察，如果某人总在谈论营收，试图说服你会暴富，或者无论如何都会成功……这种创始人是不可能建立真正大公司的。看看所有人，无论是……你和Brian Chesky共事过，我相信他就体现了这一点。Square的Jack，DoorDash的Tony，Google的Larry，Facebook的Mark，他们都关心如何取胜。他们会赢得胜利，钱自然会随之而来，但这只是副产品，不是他们追求的核心目标。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's a good segue. A question I wanted to talk about is when someone's looking for a company to join, knowing that you've worked at a lot of really successful companies, what else should people look for when they're trying to decide where to go? So what we've talked about so far is, a founder that really wants to win and is really driven, and then a problem that you want to solve? Is there anything else?
turns.zh: 真是个巧妙的过渡。我想谈论的一个问题是，当有人在寻找加入的公司时，既然你曾在许多非常成功的公司工作过，那么人们在决定去向时还应该关注哪些方面？到目前为止，我们讨论了两点：一位真正渴望获胜且充满动力的创始人，以及你想要解决的问题。还有其他要点吗？

turns.speaker: Gokul Rajaram
turns.en: I think those are the two things. One thing to look at, I would say, is that it is important to see if this company can become the number one player in its segment. I'll give you an example. I convinced someone who's going to take a very senior role, let's just say a tier two or tier three e-commerce company, to become a, not... So, basically take one step down at different company, which is at Coinbase, basically. I sat on the board of Coinbase, and I think that person still thanks me because I think they were focused too much on the title, that they were going to be the super senior person at this company on the management team, et cetera. But I said, "Ultimately you don't realize this, but the value of working at a leader in any space, the quality of talent you work with, the brand, the network effect, so many things accrue to you. I would much rather be the number two or number three person." (00:11:25): If you think of it that way, and the leader in a space, than the top person. Say Google versus Yahoo. I saw even if you're the VP of product at Yahoo or the head of product at Yahoo versus a ICPM at Google, you probably want to be the ICPM at Google. I bet you all day long, all day long. Yahoo is a great company, but Google is just a different caliber and different class. So I think it's very important to try to work at, obviously you don't know who the winner is, but if you think that's that something is a winner in a space, in large space, so many benefits that recruit from working at winners. You get unfair brand halo because you worked at a winner. People attribute a lot of the... "Oh yeah, you worked at a winner. Hence, you must be a winner." Probably not the case, but you can... I'll take it.
turns.zh:
我认为这就是关键所在。首先要看这家公司能否成为所在领域的头号玩家。我举个例子。我曾说服一位即将加入某二、三线电商公司的资深高管转投Coinbase。这家公司虽然级别低些，但其领导团队和品牌效应对他而言更有价值。人们往往过于执着于头衔，比如想成为管理团队中的超级高管之类的，但我告诉他："你现在可能没意识到，但在任何领域的领导者身边工作，与你共事的人才质量、品牌影响力、网络效应等多重优势都会对你产生深远影响。我宁愿做二号人物，也不愿当三号人物。"
(00:11:25): 以此类推，选择领域领导者而非普通公司。比如谷歌与雅虎相比。即便你是雅虎的产品副总裁或产品负责人，与谷歌的ICPM相比，你大概也会选择谷歌的ICPM。我敢打赌，日复一日，你都会这么想。雅虎固然出色，但谷歌的层次和档次完全不同。因此，努力加入领域领军者至关重要。显然你无法预知谁会成为赢家，但如果你认为某个领域的某家公司注定成功，从他们身上能获得诸多益处。加入赢家公司会附带光环效应——人们会认为"你曾在赢家公司工作，所以你本身也是赢家"。这未必属实，但你可以借此提升自身价值。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So along those lines and kind of touching on your investor experience, what should folks look for to think about, is this going to be a winner? Or should they maybe join when it's like a series B, series C when it's kind of clear that it's doing well? Do you have any thoughts? Maybe for either a new person joining the workforce, maybe PM, let's say, or even later?
turns.zh: 回到投资者经验层面，当人们考虑加入某家公司时，该关注哪些方面？比如判断这家公司是否会成为赢家？又或者是否应该在B轮、C轮融资后加入，届时公司发展态势已明朗？你有什么见解吗？无论是初入职场的新人，比如产品经理，还是更资深的从业者，都适用这些思考。

turns.speaker: Gokul Rajaram
turns.en: Personally, I feel like Hunter Walk wrote a very good post on it. He said that people who are joining the workforce new should generally join mid-stage companies because mid-stage companies you get some mentorship and it's not just basically whatever needs to be done and ultimately you don't build any deep skills. So mid-stage company I would define as something that is a multi hundred person company, but not maybe a thousand person company. (00:12:46): Somewhere from 300 to 500 people that has not just reached product market fit, but product market, channel fit. And the first product ideally is, the current product is on the way to becoming almost bulletproof. It's going to be a very, very strong product. And then it's really a path to becoming a platform beyond a product, where the company's thinking about, "How do I become a platform?" They have multiple products that serve the same customer, different problems, and they all complement and interlock with each other. (00:13:12): So because, looking back on a career, always without really thinking about it, as employee number six, seven or 800 at Google, employee number, few hundreds at Facebook, employee number seven, 800 at Square. DoorDash was slightly later because just through an acquisition. So it was like I think 1,500 or something like all around. But DoorDash also, I think, yeah, but I think that's basically, at least for me, has worked. (00:13:35): And this is even when I was not a newbie, as I was in my career. So it's really a good spot I feel if you're joining a company. For many reasons.
turns.zh:
就我个人而言，我觉得Hunter Walk写了一篇非常好的文章。他提到，刚加入职场的新人通常应该选择处于发展中期的公司加入，因为在这种公司里，你能获得一些指导，而不只是被动地完成任务，最终也无法掌握深层技能。所以我对处于发展中期的公司的定义是，员工规模在数百人但不超过千人的公司。（00:12:46）：这种公司规模通常在300至500人之间，它们不仅达到了产品市场匹配阶段，更实现了产品与市场、渠道的深度融合。理想情况下，第一款产品已经接近无懈可击的状态，将成为一款极其强大的产品。随后，公司会致力于从产品延伸到平台层面——思考如何打造一个平台型业务。多个产品服务同一客户群体，解决不同痛点，彼此互补、相互协同。

（00:13:12）：回顾我的职业生涯，我在谷歌时是第6、7或800号员工，在Facebook是几百号员工，在Square是第7、800号员工。DoorDash是通过收购加入的，当时规模约1500人左右。但就我个人而言，选择DoorDash这样的公司确实行之有效。

（00:13:35）：即便我当时已非新手，但这些经验对任何刚加入新公司的职场人同样适用。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And this advice is for, you're saying new people but also maybe people further along in their career?
turns.zh: 那这建议是针对新人的，还是可能也适用于职业生涯更成熟的人？

turns.speaker: Gokul Rajaram
turns.en: I think unless you know the founders very, very, very well, joining a very early stage company is, especially now for the next one or two years, it's going to be a brutal market out there. So you've got to be really careful. There's going to be the days of raising around, few weeks after raising your prior round, of couple of months without much movement, without much company progress have... Are probably gone for most companies. And we all have seen now companies that have raised round at crazy valuations, deflate or die quickly. And so that's happened very quickly. You might just join and your company could die a week from now. So I think the other one is to really look at the financials and really understand that better.
turns.zh: 我觉得除非你和创始人关系极其亲密，否则加入初创公司，尤其是未来一两年内的新兴公司，市场环境会非常残酷。所以必须谨慎考虑。很多公司在上一轮融资结束几周后，就会陷入数月停滞不前，毫无进展的境地。这对大多数公司来说已成常态。我们都见过估值极高融资后很快崩盘甚至倒闭的公司。这种情况转瞬即逝。你可能刚加入，公司一周后就倒闭了。所以另一条建议是，务必仔细审视财务数据，深入理解其中的奥秘。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. That's really helpful advice. You mentioned Brian Armstrong, Brian Chesky and some of the other folks that you have worked with and gotten to know. I'm curious, of the companies you've worked at, say now Coinbase, on the board, Google, Facebook, Square, DoorDash, what are some things that have kind of stuck with you? (00:14:46): Things you've taken away about how to run a company, build a product? Or anything else that's just taught you a lesson about how to do what you're doing?
turns.zh: 太棒了。这真是非常有用的建议。你提到了布莱恩·阿姆斯特朗、布莱恩·切斯基等你共事过且熟识的人。我很好奇，在你工作过的公司中，比如现在在Coinbase的董事会、谷歌、Facebook、Square、DoorDash，有哪些经验教训让你受益匪浅？（00:14:46）：比如如何运营公司、打造产品的经验？或者其他任何能让你在当前工作中获益的教训？

turns.speaker: Gokul Rajaram
turns.en: One of the most interesting things I've realized is there are multiple paths to greatness. What I mean by that is if I were to look at one word to describe each of the companies I have actually worked at. Google would be technical. It is very, very technical, technology focused, because Google believe, if you build great technology, they will come. Facebook was very growth focused. Very much, here's a goal, we want to hit 1 billion MAUs, let's work backwards from there. Square was very design focused. Let's build the cleanest minimalistic design, the most well designed product, then good things happen. DoorDash by nature is more operational, probably the right word to use where product and operational intertwined. Uber probably is the same word. So I think there are multiple paths to greatness, but I think the founder and market fit in terms of even the type of company that's needed is very strong. (00:15:46): In other words, I think founders have to be authentic to themselves. The other thing I saw is that each founder, whether it's Tony Shoe at DoorDash or Jack, they all had their distinctive styles but they didn't try to change their style. In some ways the company was built almost in their image in some ways and that was fine. I think if you try to build a company that's inauthentic to who you are as a founder, that's not going to work. So ultimately you want to... If Jack tried to build a company that sold enterprise software, I don't think that would've worked. That's not who he is. And so you want a founder and a company culture that are essentially synonymous and founders to be authentic. And I think finally the one other thing that I've seen is, the product itself ideally needs to have some remarkability. (00:16:33): What I mean by that is, it needs to be better than anything else that solves that pain point along a few dimensions that really matter, even if it's worse along other dimensions. So I think every great product, it needs to have a lot of word of mouth. I think especially nowadays, I'm seeing a lot of consumer companies challenged because they relied on Facebook or paid media to drive customer acquisition, and bunch of young companies are coming to me saying, "What do we do now?" (00:17:01): I'm like, "Look, the biggest thing you did wrong initially was you didn't pay enough attention to organic growth. Basically, was this product compelling enough that people talk about it and bring other people along? And you completely relied on paid and that's coming back to bite you." (00:17:16): So a good metric is that 40 to 50% of your new customers should ideally come from organic channels and 50% from paid. If 90% come from paid, that means at some point that the music is going to stop.
turns.zh:
我意识到的最有趣的一点是，通往伟大的道路有多种可能性。我的意思是，如果要用一个词来描述我曾任职过的每家公司：谷歌是技术导向型——它非常注重技术，因为谷歌相信，如果你能打造出卓越的技术，用户自然会涌入；Facebook则极度注重增长——比如设定10亿月活用户的目标，然后倒推实现路径；Square则以设计为核心——致力于打造极简设计、精良的产品；DoorDash本质上更偏向运营，产品与运营深度融合；优步可能也是同样的风格。所以我认为通往伟大的道路有多种可能性，但创始人与市场契合度（甚至所需公司的类型）至关重要。

（00:15:46）：换句话说，创始人必须忠实于自我。我还发现，每位创始人——无论是DoorDash的托尼·肖还是优步的杰克——都有独特的风格，但他们从不试图改变自我。在某种程度上，公司几乎是以他们的形象塑造而成的，这没问题。但如果你试图打造一个与创始人格格不入的公司，那注定失败。因此，最终你需要……如果杰克试图创办一家销售企业软件的公司，我认为那行不通。这不是他本质所长。所以创始人和公司文化必须高度契合，创始人必须保持真实。

（00:16:33）：最后我发现，最理想的产品必须具备显著的差异化。我指的是，它在关键维度上要优于其他同类解决方案，即便在其他维度上稍逊一筹。比如，每款伟大的产品都需要口碑传播。如今很多消费类公司正面临挑战，因为它们依赖Facebook或付费广告获取用户，而许多年轻公司来找我问：“现在该怎么办？” 

（00:17:01）：我会说：“看，你们最初犯的最大错误就是对自然增长重视不足。基本上，产品是否足够吸引人，让人们主动推荐并吸引更多用户？而你们完全依赖付费推广，这最终会反噬你们。” 

（00:17:16）：所以一个好的指标是：40%至50%的新用户应来自自然渠道，50%来自付费推广。如果90%来自付费推广，那意味着终局即将到来。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Unless you've got some magical insight or someone that's just killing it.
turns.zh: 除非你有某种神奇的洞察力，或者某个公司正在大获成功。

turns.speaker: Gokul Rajaram
turns.en: A growth pack, right? Everyone's looking at this growth tag, but there is no... There's nothing like the silver growth tag bullet.
turns.zh: 增长包，对吧？每个人都在关注这个增长标签，但根本没有……没有像银色增长标签那样实用的指标。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's interesting, there are a couple companies I'm an investor in that are actually still working really well through paid. And so it's definitely possible but incredibly hard.
turns.zh: 有趣的是，我投资的几家公司实际上仍在通过付费推广取得良好效果。当然这是可能的，但极其困难。

turns.speaker: Gokul Rajaram
turns.en: Yeah, those are exceptions that prove the rule.
turns.zh: 是的，这些都是例外，但它们印证了这个规律。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What I think of when you talk about this is that something Seth Godin shared a while ago that I always come back to you, this idea that your product has to be remarkable where people want to remark on it, for it to have a chance, especially in consumer, because that's how things start to grow. People just can't help but talk about it.
turns.zh: 每当你谈及这个话题时，我脑海中浮现的便是赛斯·高丁不久前分享的一个观点——我总会反复向你提及这个理念：要想让产品真正获得成功，尤其是在消费领域，关键在于让产品足够引人注目，足以引发人们的议论。毕竟，口口相传才是推动产品发展的不二法门。

turns.speaker: Gokul Rajaram
turns.en: Exactly. Very well said.
turns.zh: 确实如此。说得太好了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Easier said than done. Okay, so getting a little tactical. I'm curious to get your take on just the product development process at companies. How do you think about founders setting up a product development process? What do you recommend usually? And then maybe further down the line, when they get to like 25 people, maybe 50 people, how do you advise founders think about their product development process in the early stages and then as they evolve?
turns.zh: 说起来容易做起来难。好吧，现在来谈点实际操作层面的东西。我很想听听你对企业产品开发流程的看法。你认为创始人在建立产品开发流程时应该如何考虑？通常你会给出哪些建议？再往后延伸一下，当企业发展到25人、50人这样的规模时，你会如何指导创始人在初期和发展过程中优化产品开发流程？

turns.speaker: Gokul Rajaram
turns.en: I think first of all, the planning period is different at the very early stage. At the very early stage, it needs to be a weekly plan, where while as you grow the granularity, you still need weekly plans, but you also need quarterly plans that wrap around that. You start with quarterly goals. In fact, I was talking to a series A company and they were just starting the first several quarterly plan. They just did series A round, so they need to plan at a quarterly level and then it translates back into the weekly level. When you're very young, you're literally going week to week. And then once you become much bigger, you get to annual planning, which then leads to quarterly goals and so on. So the granularity is different. The second thing is the tools you actually use. I think initially you just have a very simple spreadsheet. (00:19:13): I am a big believer that you can have all these fancy project management tools. Whenever I've been a leader in a product team, I've never imposed a certain tool because I feel different PMs and teams find the right tool for them. It's about keeping it super simple. If you have too many complex tools, people don't know how to use them. Engineering teams typically use something like Jira, and as a product person you don't want another complex tool for them to use to figure out things. So a simple spreadsheet, and your founder that you update with things to do and people who are going to do it. And then that's basically it. I think as you grow, you start wanting to write a little bit more surviving, the first thing you start doing. And then as a very young company, you don't have a separate product strategy from a company strategy. (00:19:55): The product and company strategy are the same. As you start growing, you have a go-to market strategy, product strategy, et cetera, et cetera. So you start more clearly separating out the company strategy from the product strategy. The first thing you start seeing is when a product manager joins... So I think of course what happens is that the 25 person status, you have a PM who sometimes joins the company. I think the right time for PMs to join the company is about eight to 10 engineers or so. Anywhere between five and 10. But 10 engineers is... Unless the founder themselves wants to be the PM, but that's when you start seeing a professional PM join and the PM typically wants to clearly articulate. Good PMs want to articulate what the product strategy is based on company strategy. So you start seeing the emergence of a separate product strategy doc that is written at the 20, 23 person stage, and the product strategy then makes choices. What customers are we serving? More clearly articulates what have been implicit hopefully earlier. (00:20:51): And then that guides product development. And then I think when you get really large, you have essentially multiple interlocking products that there are multiple product strategy docs. And then you get into more cross functional strategy docs, into product strategy doc, et cetera. But I think at the very core of it, there are two things. One, the team still needs to meet on a daily basis. There is a standup cadence, and that atomic team of six, seven people, which is engineers, product person, designer, hopefully an analyst, they are the product development team. And they still review the tasks on a weekly basis, but where it emanates from when you're young, it doesn't have any roots. It's literally, they're just living and dying on a week by week basis, trying different things till they get product market fit. (00:21:38): As you go bigger and you have product market fit, you start building plans around that. And these iterations, these sprints then emanate working back from the goals that you set on a quarterly basis.
turns.zh:
我认为首先，在早期阶段，规划周期是不同的。在早期阶段，需要制定每周计划。随着公司发展壮大，虽然每周计划仍是必需，但同时也需要制定季度计划来统筹全局。你从季度目标入手。我曾与一家A轮融资的公司交流，他们刚刚开始制定首批季度计划。刚完成A轮融资后，他们需要从季度层面进行规划，再将其转化为每周行动指南。当公司规模很小时，规划周期短至每周一次；而当公司规模扩大后，则转向年度规划，再细化为季度目标等。这体现了规划粒度的差异。

其次，关于实际使用的工具。我认为初期可以使用简单的电子表格。（00:19:13）我坚信不必强制推行复杂的项目管理工具。无论我作为产品团队领导时，从未强制使用特定工具，因为不同PM和团队总能找到适合自己的工具。关键在于保持简单。如果工具过于复杂，人们反而无从下手。工程团队通常使用Jira等工具，但作为产品人员，你不应为他们额外增添复杂的工具去解决问题。因此，初期只需使用简单的电子表格，由创始人更新待办事项和负责人员，基本即可。

随着公司发展壮大，产品经理开始承担更多职责。初期公司战略与产品战略并无明显区分。随着公司成长，你会逐步制定市场进入策略、产品战略等，从而明确区分公司战略与产品战略。这一转变始于产品经理加入团队时——通常在公司规模25人左右时，PM才会加入。此时加入的PM最适宜在8-10名工程师团队中工作，理想人数为5-10人。但若创始人亲自担任PM，则另当别论。此时专业PM会加入团队，他们通常会清晰阐述产品战略的制定依据——基于公司战略。因此，产品战略文档在20-23人阶段开始成形，并基于此进行产品开发决策。

当公司规模进一步扩大，多款产品相互关联时，产品战略文档将分层细化。此外，跨职能战略文档也将应运而生。但核心要点在于：团队仍需每日开会（站会），核心六、七人团队（工程师、产品经理、设计师、分析师）每周复盘任务。早期阶段的规划缺乏根基，纯粹是每周试错，直至产品市场契合。
待公司规模逐渐扩大，且产品与市场契合度提升后，你便会据此制定发展规划。而这些迭代过程、这些冲刺阶段，最终都将围绕你每季度设定的目标展开。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow. So much good advice. There's a couple things I want to follow up on there. What are some common pitfalls you've seen in startups trying to set up product development processes or the way they build product? What do you find are some of the more common mistakes that founders make? That early teams make?
turns.zh: 哇，真是太多的好建议了。这里有几点我想深入探讨一下。你们在初创公司中看到过哪些常见的陷阱，比如在建立产品开发流程或产品构建方式时遇到的问题？创始人最常犯的错误有哪些？早期团队又会犯哪些错误？

turns.speaker: Gokul Rajaram
turns.en: The biggest one I think is, the founder becomes too tactical and disempowers their team. I think the founder thinks they know what customers want. I think they don't empower their teams enough and they basically just tell the engineers what to build. And I think that leads to teams that are basically tactically just shaping feature after feature without truly solving problems. And I think that then creeps into when you hire a PM, they see this is how the company's working and they then also start working the same way. I think the best founders early on trust their engineering teams and product development teams to solve problems and more clearly present a problem to them and help them. And this is true for PMs also. They help them brainstorm solutions and try to work with the team to understand why we chose a certain solution versus another solution. And then the team feels empowered to go build it versus it dictating them. (00:23:00): Why should we build an iOS app, while the actual problem to solve is we want to increase the percentage of people using a service to five times a week versus two times a week. And building an iOS app is one tactic, but there are many other tactics. Which is improving our web experience, et cetera. So decision making and transparency of decisions around how products change customer behavior is probably the... And that leads to the culture of what is called a feature factory, where product teams basically are very proud of shaping feature after feature without truly knowing how much impact the feature has. If a feature is shipped, but it doesn't change customer behavior at all, is it really a feature or no? It's like a tree falling in the forest.
turns.zh: 我认为最大的问题是，创始人变得过于关注战术细节，从而剥夺了团队的自主权。我觉得创始人总认为自己知道客户想要什么。他们没有充分授权团队，基本上就是直接告诉工程师该开发什么功能。这会导致团队只是机械地一个接一个地开发功能，却无法真正解决问题。当你招聘产品经理时，这种问题也会延续下去，因为他们看到公司就是这样运作的，于是也开始沿用同样的模式。我认为优秀的创始人早期会信任工程团队和产品开发团队，让他们去解决问题，并清晰地向团队阐明问题所在。这对产品经理同样适用——产品经理会帮助团队头脑风暴解决方案，并与团队共同探讨为何选择某种方案而非其他方案。这样团队就能主动去开发，而非被动接受指令。（00:23:00）比如，用户真正需要解决的问题是如何让每周使用服务的人数从两次提升至五次，但创始人却偏要先开发iOS应用。这只是其中一种战术，实际上还有许多其他选择，比如优化网页体验等。因此，围绕产品如何改变客户行为的决策制定和决策透明度可能是关键所在……这会导致所谓“功能工厂”的文化，产品团队往往为开发一个又一个功能而自豪，却从未真正评估这些功能的实际影响。如果功能上线却未能改变客户行为，那它还算功能吗？这就像森林里倒了一棵树，却无人知晓。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh my god, I love that. And I've definitely seen these teams that you're talking about and that only becomes worse once they hire a PM. I like your rule of thumb of hiring a PM when you've gotten eight to 10 engineers. What points to it's time to hire a PM, other than that? Is there other things you've seen of just like, "Oh my god, this team really needs a PM," or they should wait longer? What have you seen there?
turns.zh: 天哪，我太赞同了。我确实见过你描述的那些团队，而且一旦招聘了产品经理，情况往往会更糟。我很认同你提到的招聘PM的经验法则——当团队有8到10名工程师时再考虑。除了这个，还有哪些迹象表明该招聘PM了？有没有其他情况让你感叹“天哪，这个团队真的需要PM”？或者认为应该再等一阵子？你见过哪些典型案例？

turns.speaker: Gokul Rajaram
turns.en: I always feel that you should hire to solve a problem you're facing. You should never hire... Or you feel you're going to face. But especially I think just over-hiring, especially... You want to be efficient and smaller teams are always good. Smaller companies are always good, part of the problem. So there are many teams. First of all, the question is if the founder is able to play the role, someone needs to play the role of a product manager. If the founder is able to and willing to play the role of product manager. The problem is with eight to 10 engineers, if the founder is doing other things besides playing the role of a product manager, then the eight to 10 person engineering team is not being cared for and fed. (00:24:39): Engineers are by far the most expensive resources in the company. By far, right? I mean if you look at the composition of engineers versus... And PMs versus any other function, it's two to three, equity, cash, everything. (00:24:52): And if you think of it that way, then if you're not caring and feeding and not leveraging this amazing most expensive resource, well, that's a crime. That's a crime. In some ways you got to think about yourself. Am I, as the founder, is this 10 person team or 8 person team being leveraged? Are they solving the right problems? Do they know how to brainstorm? Do they know how to solve problems? Do I have the bandwidth to sit with them and present the right problems, talk to customers, figure out the right sequencing, the right prioritization of problems to work on, et cetera? (00:25:25): And if you're not able to do that, you've got to have someone who can do that full time. And it might be someone from the team. I mean there are two... We can talk about how to hire your first PM and there are many, many-
turns.zh: 我一直觉得，招聘人才来解决你面临的难题是没问题的。但绝不要为了预防可能出现的问题而提前招人。尤其是过度招人这种做法，我认为弊大于利。团队规模越小越高效，公司规模越小越灵活——这也是部分创业公司遇到问题的根源。首先，创始人是否有能力胜任产品经理的角色？如果创始人既有意愿又有能力担任产品经理，那再考虑团队规模。若团队规模为8到10名工程师，而创始人却在分心做其他事，那这支工程团队就得不到有效管理和资源支持。（00:24:39）：工程师是公司里最昂贵的资源。说真的，如果你看看工程师与其他职位的比例，比如产品经理与其他职位的比例，通常是2比3——股权、现金、资源投入各方面都存在巨大差距。（00:24:52）：从这个角度看，如果你不去管理和支持这支最宝贵的资源，那简直就是犯罪。犯罪行为！作为创始人，你得审视自己：这支10人或8人的团队是否得到了充分利用？他们是否在解决正确的问题？他们会头脑风暴吗？他们会解决问题吗？我是否有足够的时间和精力与他们一起确定正确的研发方向、与客户沟通、规划问题的优先级顺序等等？（00:25:25）：如果做不到这些，就必须找个全职的专业人士来负责。这人可能来自团队内部。我们可以聊聊如何招聘首位产品经理，这方面有很多经验之谈。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, let's do it. I definitely wanted to ask that. I know you wrote a great post about this, just how to actually hire your great PM and you have a strong opinion about that.
turns.zh: 好的，我们来探讨一下这个话题。我知道你写过一篇很棒的文章，详细讲解了如何招聘优秀的产品经理，你对这方面的见解很深刻。

turns.speaker: Gokul Rajaram
turns.en: Yeah, I have a strong opinion and it might be just based on every single company I've been at. The first PM at every company has been someone who's either been an analyst or an engineer or a designer who's worked there already and they just move from their role to being a PM. Why? Because many cases, the role of the PM is actually to be the liaison between the founder, founders and the engineering team. And so it needs to be someone that the founders trust and the engineering team trusts and also they know how the founders and the engineering team work. (00:26:16): And many times if you bring a PM from the outside with a completely different process, many times the organ can be rejected by the body. And so they may not be the best PM you could get in terms of just functional skills, but they would be the best PM from a cultural assimilation. And getting the engineers just to understand the value of a PM and getting the founders to be comfortable, slowly being more hands off. Was it true of Airbnb, also? Was Joe not the first PM?
turns.zh: 是的，我确实有自己的看法，这可能源于我曾待过的每家公司。每家公司的首位产品经理，要么是已经在公司任职的分析师、工程师或设计师，然后从原有岗位转任产品经理。为什么？因为产品经理的核心角色往往是创始人与工程团队之间的桥梁。因此，首位产品经理必须得到创始人和工程团队的信任，同时要理解他们的工作方式。（00:26:16）：很多时候，如果从外部引入产品经理，带来完全不同的工作流程，往往会遭到团队的排斥。这样的产品经理或许在专业技能上并非最出色，但从文化融合角度来看，却是最佳人选。让工程师们认识到产品经理的价值，让创始人逐渐放权，这对团队发展至关重要。Airbnb也是如此吗？乔（Joe）不是首位产品经理吗？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: He was. And he was actually an engineer when he joined, so that's exactly how you describe. So say that you hire, or you transition someone from PM into their... Being the first PM. What are some signs that maybe they're not doing too well and things aren't going well and maybe you should go in a different direction?
turns.zh: 没错。他加入时就是工程师，这正是你所描述的典型案例。那么，当你招聘或让某人从产品经理转型为首位产品经理时，如何判断他们是否表现不佳、工作进展不顺，需要调整方向呢？

turns.speaker: Gokul Rajaram
turns.en: I think the biggest one is I always feel with PMs it's actually two or three things you can look at. One is, you can actually just ask the engineers themselves. Engineers are fairly blunt. And when I manage PMs, I've seen that they always tell me... Engineering managers in particular, they're very, very quick to tell you, "Look, this person is not working, they're not being effective." (00:27:27): What value are they adding? And I think just number one thing you have to do is you have to, just because you hire a PM doesn't... You can't abdicate that responsibility of understanding how the team is doing. It's not gone. You've got to talk to the engineers and designers constantly to see, is the product manager adding value? Second, if you see the PM, the newly anointed PM still get too much into the how to build the product, which is really the domain of the engineers and designers. (00:27:53): See? That's the other failure case where you've got to... And this is something through coaching comes. Obviously they just were an engineer or designer two weeks ago and now they are a PM. There's a immediate impulse to start going back into their comfort zone. And the key is to really push them to go more strongly biased towards customers and push them more towards talking to customers, understanding customer problems. And I think every PM, we all know this, all of us as PMs, there was no class to be a PM. So there are some people who joined APM programs directly out of school, but most of us are engineers, marketers, analysts, designers. And we became PMs after that. So we all come with inherent biases and ways of doing things and it's only a function of how long it takes us to shed... Or at least to not be that persona, but to actually take on a PM persona. (00:28:45): And so I personally believe in the growth mindset a lot. The reason that hopefully this person was chosen to be the PM is the founder saw that this person has the characteristics, traits, which is curiosity, the customer centricity, communication skills, being able to facilitate discussion, all of those things that a PM should have. Problem solving skills. And so hopefully those are things they didn't just pick a random engineer out of the 10, but they picked the right engineer, the right designer. And I think if you do that and you surround them with some good mentors, I think in six months they'll make good PMs.
turns.zh: 我认为最重要的一点是，面对产品经理时，你其实可以从两个或三个方面去审视。首先，你可以直接询问工程师本人。工程师们通常比较直言不讳。当我管理产品经理时，我发现他们总是对我说……尤其是工程经理，他们会很快指出：“看，这个人工作效率低下，成效不佳。”（00:27:27）：他们能创造什么价值？我认为你首先必须做的是，即便聘请了产品经理，也不能推卸掉了解团队运作状况的责任。这份责任并不会消失。你必须不断与工程师和设计师沟通，观察产品经理是否真正在创造价值。其次，如果你发现新晋产品经理过度沉浸于产品构建细节，而这本应是工程师和设计师的专属领域。（00:27:53）：看到了吧？这就是另一种失败案例，你必须……这需要通过辅导来解决。显然，他们两周前还是工程师或设计师，现在就成了产品经理。他们会不由自主地回到舒适区。关键在于，要真正推动他们更偏向客户视角，更多地与客户沟通，理解客户痛点。我们都知道，成为产品经理没有固定课程。有些人直接从学校进入APM项目，但大多数人原本是工程师、市场营销人员、分析师或设计师。成为产品经理后，我们都带着固有偏见和做事方式，需要花时间摒弃这些习惯，或至少摆脱原有角色，真正融入产品经理的角色。（00:28:45）：所以我个人非常推崇成长型思维。产品经理之所以被选中，是因为创始人看到了这个人具备好奇心、以客户为中心、沟通技巧、推动讨论的能力等产品经理应有的特质。还有解决问题的能力。所以希望公司不是随机挑选工程师或设计师，而是选对了人。只要辅导到位，再加上优秀的导师指导，我相信他们六个月内就能成为优秀的产品经理。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that. Maybe just try randomly. You never know.
turns.zh: 我喜欢这种做法。或许可以随机尝试一下。谁知道呢。

turns.speaker: Gokul Rajaram
turns.en: Good work.
turns.zh: 干得好。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Just to close the loop on the idea of when it's time to hire a PM, somebody may be listening to this and feeling like, "Oh, we got to get a PM in ASAP." What are some signs or reasons to wait a little bit longer before you hire your first PM?
turns.zh: 最后再总结一下关于何时该聘请产品经理的观点，也许有人听了这段话会觉得：“哦，我们得尽快找个产品经理。” 那么，有哪些迹象或理由说明不妨再等一等再聘请首位产品经理呢？

turns.speaker: Gokul Rajaram
turns.en: If everything is going well? In other words, if your product team is clicking, if they're empowered and if you feel that they can take problems that you're giving them, not just tactics, but they're able to take a problem. Hey, we need to improve new user acquisition and the product team, the whatever, your product development team, which is just engineers able to take that and essentially act on it and suggest three different ways to improve user acquisition. (00:30:04): For example, choose the one that has the best ROI, how you measure it, and then execute on that and then run a test to say, "Look, it did improve user acquisition?" That's a well defined product team. So I think you need an empowered product team that takes ownership and can take a problem, figure out all the options to solve the problem and then prioritize them. And so if you feel that's happening, you don't need a PM. But I've seen that it's hard as engineering teams grow. To engineers, I think they do need that partner. They really that partner to help facilitate that for the most part.
turns.zh: 若一切进展顺利？换句话说，如果你的产品团队运作良好，他们获得了充分授权，并且你认为他们能够处理你交给他们的难题——不只是制定战术，而是能真正解决问题。比如，"我们需要提升新用户获取量"，产品团队（无论是工程师还是其他成员）都能够接手这个任务，提出三种提升用户获取的方案。（00:30:04）：比如，选择ROI最高的方案，衡量效果，再付诸实践并进行测试，验证是否确实提升了用户获取量。这才是高效运作的产品团队。所以我认为，你需要一个被充分授权、能够自主承担问题、探索多种解决方案并进行优先级排序的产品团队。如果你感觉团队达到了这种状态，那就无需PM。但我发现，随着工程团队规模扩大，PM的需求往往会增加。对工程师而言，他们确实需要PM作为合作伙伴，帮助他们高效推进工作。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's awesome advice. And yeah, I think that's going to be-
turns.zh: 这真是很棒的建议。是的，我认为这将成为——

turns.speaker: Gokul Rajaram
turns.en: I think infrastructure is a great example. I think Stripe for example, is famous for not hiring PMs because I think when your audience is developers, they know their audience really well. And so I think many dev ops and developer facing companies, they don't have that many PMs. The PM to engineering ratio is very small. Even in Stripe today I bet it's much smaller than other companies. So those are exceptions that engineers truly understand the domain better. So the machine learning companies, infrastructure companies generally I think need fewer PMs. And this is true for any consumer product company. I bet Airbnb's infrastructure team had zero PMs, or very few PMs because they are serving other engineers. So I think those products, I think you need much fewer PMs than consumer facing products.
turns.zh: 基础设施领域就是一个很好的例子。比如Stripe就以不招聘PM而闻名，因为当你的用户群体是开发者时，他们对用户需求非常了解。因此，我认为许多面向开发者的公司，比如DevOps和开发者服务公司，PM数量非常少。PM与工程师的比例很低。即使在今天的Stripe，我敢打赌他们的PM比例也远低于其他公司。所以这些例外情况下，工程师确实更了解业务领域。因此，机器学习公司、基础设施公司通常需要较少的PM。这对任何面向消费者的产品公司都适用。我敢打赌Airbnb的基础设施团队没有PM，或者只有极少数PM，因为他们服务的是其他工程师。所以对于这类产品，我认为需要的PM比面向消费者的产品少得多。
