I think Snapchat had like 200 people also, but I think it's because their designers basically played the role of a PM.
turns.zh: 本期节目由Productboard赞助。产品领导者信赖Productboard，助力团队打造重要产品。从初创公司到行业巨头，超过6,000家公司依赖Productboard更快地将正确的产品推向市场，包括Zoom、福特、UI Path和先锋基金等公司。Productboard可帮助你创建可扩展、透明且标准化的流程，让PM们了解客户真正需求，进而优先构建下一步功能。（00:31:56）：利益相关方也能感受到其价值，通过易于查看且自动更新的路线图，每个人都能了解你们在做什么以及为什么这么做。制定数据驱动的产品决策，提升收入和用户采用率，赋能产品团队创造令人愉悦的客户体验。访问Productboard.com了解更多信息。（00:32:15）：是的，我写过一篇文章，里面有一张表格，列出了各公司获得首位PM前等待的时间。Snapchat也有200人，但我认为这是因为他们的设计师基本上充当了PM的角色。

turns.speaker: Gokul Rajaram
turns.en: There we go, that's right. The designers played the role of the PM.
turns.zh: 没错，就是这样。设计师们充当了PM的角色。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Somebody's got to be doing the job, right? Hopefully they enjoy it, sometimes they don't.
turns.zh: 总得有人做这些工作，对吧？希望他们能乐在其中，当然有时并非如此。

turns.speaker: Gokul Rajaram
turns.en: That's right.
turns.zh: 没错。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. So say you've hired your first PM, you're building a product team. Something I wanted to get your take on is, as PM teams grow, sometimes they end up changing who they're reporting to. Sometimes it ends up being a CPO, sometimes a GM, sometimes like even a CTO in some cases. Do you have any thoughts on when it makes sense for product teams to report to say a GM versus a chief product officer or something else? Do you have any advice there?
turns.zh: 好的。假设你刚聘请了首位产品经理，正在组建产品团队。我想听听你的看法：随着产品团队规模扩大，他们汇报对象往往会发生变化。有时是首席产品官，有时是总经理，甚至在某些情况下是首席技术官。对于产品团队来说，向总经理汇报还是向首席产品官汇报更合理？你对此有什么建议吗？

turns.speaker: Gokul Rajaram
turns.en: Yeah, I've worked at companies where it's both functional, products orgs are functional. Where all the PMs report into the head of product, reports to a CEO, as well as a GM structure where PMs report into a GM, as do an engineering leader and a design leader and even a sales leader, marketing leader, et cetera. So both can work, but ultimately you want, I do think once you have three to four PMs, you do want those three to four PMs to report to a functional product leader just because I feel they want a mentor, first of all. They want a coach. And you want to build a product culture and hopefully discipline across those four or five PMs because the leverage you get. Someone said this, I think a few years ago, I remember this, engineers are obviously very important to hire, but a bad PM... You can get incredible errors from a good PM, but a bad PM can really screw up, can screw up the work of 10 engineers. (00:34:01): So it's much more important to hire good PM than it is to hire a good engineer. Any good one. Because there's so few PMs for every engineer, that one good or bad PM can really screw up everything, compared to the impact of one good or bad engineer. So what that means for me is that if you have four or five PMs, and the one way to up level them is to actually make sure the four together are sharing best practices, learning, hopefully building a culture. And I think it's hard for a GM who's also managing other functions to do that. (00:34:32): So I would say yes, maybe one or two PMs could report into a CEO or a GM or someone else, but once you get into a four or five PM team, they probably should report to a dedicated of product manager whose job is to be a mentor, be a coach, attract strong new folks to the team, hire, build a strong culture, et cetera, et cetera. (00:34:57): That product manager, I think they could report to the CTO, they could report to the CEO, they could report to the GM. I don't think that matters. But the ICPMs is what I'm more worried about. Who do they report into? I think they should report into a dedicated manager once it gets a certain size.
turns.zh: 是的，我曾在一些公司工作过，那里既有职能型产品组织，所有产品经理都向产品负责人汇报，也有总经理模式，产品经理向总经理汇报，同时向工程总监、设计总监甚至销售总监汇报。两种模式都可行，但一旦团队有三到四名产品经理，我认为他们应该向专职产品负责人汇报，因为他们首先需要导师和指导者。此外，培养产品文化和纪律性也很重要，这样能发挥团队的协同效应。正如有人几年前说过，工程师固然重要，但一个糟糕的产品经理可能会毁掉10个工程师的工作。（00:34:01）因此，聘请优秀的产品经理比优秀的工程师更重要，因为每个工程师对应的产品经理数量很少，一个好或坏的产品经理会影响整个团队，而一个好或坏的工程师对团队的影响则较小。因此，我认为如果有四到五名产品经理，提升他们的最佳方式是确保他们共同分享最佳实践、相互学习，并努力建立团队文化。我认为总经理同时管理其他职能部门很难做到这一点。（00:34:32）所以我认为，一两名产品经理可以向CEO、总经理或其他人汇报，但一旦团队达到四到五名产品经理，他们应该向专职产品经理汇报，专职产品经理的职责是提供指导、吸引优秀人才加入团队、招聘人才、建立强大文化等。（00:34:57）这位产品经理可以向CTO、CEO或总经理汇报，我认为这无关紧要。但我更担心的是ICPM（初级产品经理），他们向谁汇报？我认为一旦团队规模达到一定程度，他们应该向专职经理汇报。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. I could not agree more. Another thing I've seen, as a lot of companies go one direction, they go GM models, then they go back to something else where it's completely business unit oriented and functional reporting and then they go back. So I found it, just try something. See if that works. You can always change it in the future. That's super common. (00:35:30): I wanted to transition to hiring, talk about hiring. You recently had this incredible thread on Twitter about how to hire a leader and I think maybe just a product leader, maybe broadly, leader. And so for folks that haven't seen that or have time to go on Twitter, I'd love to just hear your advice on how to hire a leader for a company.
turns.zh: 太棒了。我完全赞同。我还注意到，很多公司在发展过程中会尝试不同的模式，先是采用总经理模式，后来又转向完全以业务单元为导向的职能汇报模式，再转回来。因此，我认为应该多尝试，观察效果如何，未来随时可以调整。这很常见。（00:35:30）接下来我想谈谈招聘。最近你在Twitter上发了一篇关于如何招聘领导者的精彩帖子，可能不仅针对产品经理，也适用于更广泛的领导者。对于没看到那篇帖子或没时间上Twitter的人，我很想听听你对如何为公司招聘领导者的建议。

turns.speaker: Gokul Rajaram
turns.en: That post actually was triggered by, that morning, one of my company CEO messaged me that, "Wow, I hired someone from this company. How'd you know this person was available from this company?" I was like, "I didn't know about this person, I just knew this company was really good at sales. And so that's why I recommended the company." And he said, "This is the third time I hired based on advice you gave and these are all senior leaders here. How did you do that?" I'm like, "Actually, thinking about it, you're right." (00:36:19): When companies ask me... Because the number one, if you ever ask a company, "What's the thing that's keeping you up at night?" They'll always say one of the things always that's keeping them at night, "I want to hire a leader for X, Y, Z function." And I never respond with, here's a person. I'll always say, "Well, you're in this space selling to this kind of customer or serving this kind of customer. Let's think about the best in class companies, who's also, who's very good at functionally the thing you're hiring for, serving the similar type of customer." (00:36:48): And so basically that was the origin of the post. And really what it says is, in order to hire, if you want to have a playbook for hiring good leaders or strong leaders for any function, look at best of class companies or companies that are best of class at that function in the similar space. Not your competitors, but you've got to look beyond your competitors. You've got to look at folks who are serving SMBs or enterprises or whatever this... Or consumers. And then say, "Okay, I want to hire a head of marketing." Great. This is the hardest thing. Go to find the top three or four companies who are excellent at marketing to consumers. If that's what you're... Then you don't hire the person, the head of marketing at these companies. (00:37:31): You hire the person who's reporting to them, the lieutenant. And actually, Adam Zamos, who was the head of people at Square chimed into say, "At Square, early days we used to go..." He used to run people, the people team at Square. "We used to go and hire the up and coming lieutenants of the lieutenants." And so I think you basically have to build almost an org chart and it's not that hard. You just have to spend time on LinkedIn, to say who are all the people in the org? Who reports to? And you can ask some of your friends who work at a company to better construct the org chart and you just literally go through that company and pick out the people. And I saw this in practice because once Square went public, we were the only public finTech in 2015, one of the very few public fintechs. (00:38:16): And so my goodness, our teams were raided. The next two years, I literally saw the full team, a huge chunk of a team in different parts of payments, compliance, risk, just being raided by other fintechs. And I saw that this was being followed. Because you say, "Okay, who's the company who's best in being in compliance? Square." And I'm sure there are other companies also, but Square was well known because it was public and it was large, they had done it at scale, et cetera. They didn't go after our head, they went after the lieutenant and the lieutenant of the lieutenant, et cetera.
turns.zh:
那个帖子其实源于那天早上，我公司的首席执行官给我发消息说：“哇，我从这家公司招了个人。你怎么知道这家公司有合适的人选？”我回答：“我根本不认识这个人，我只是知道这家公司很擅长销售。所以我才推荐了他们。”他接着问：“这是你第三次根据我的建议招人了，而且都是这里的高层领导。你是怎么做到的？” 我说：“仔细想想，你说得对。”  

（00:36:19）：当公司问我……因为如果你问一家公司：“什么事情让你们夜不能寐？”他们总会提到一个难题：“我想为X、Y、Z职位招个领导。” 我从不直接推荐候选人，而是会说：“你们在服务这类客户，或者专注于这类职能。让我们看看业内顶尖公司，他们在功能上是否擅长于你们要招的职位？”  

（00:36:48）：这就是那篇帖子的核心思想。核心观点是，要想成功招聘，无论是任何职能的优秀领导者或强者，都要研究同行业中在该职能上表现卓越的顶尖公司——不一定是竞争对手，而是要跳出竞争视野。比如，服务中小企业、企业客户或消费者的公司。  

（00:37:31）：比如想招营销负责人。最难的部分是，先找到在消费者营销方面表现出色的前三四家公司。然后不招这些公司的营销负责人，而是招他们的下属。Square前人力资源总监Adam Zamos曾透露：“早期我们会招那些有潜力的中层管理者。” 这意味着你需要构建一个组织架构图，不算难。只需花时间在LinkedIn上查看组织架构，分析各职位汇报关系，再请教内部朋友完善图表。  

（00:38:16）：2015年Square上市时，我们是首家上市的金融科技公司。随后的两年间，整个支付、合规、风险等部门大量人才被其他金融科技公司挖走。这印证了我的观点。比如想招合规负责人，大家都会说“Square”——虽然其他公司可能更出色，但Square因上市规模大、经验丰富而备受关注。对手们不招我们的领导，而是挖走他们的下属。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I see. So you saw this happening to you and then you've weaponized it in reverse. I love it. Great advice. I've never heard this advice before and it sounds incredibly good. And so thank you for sharing all that. Thank you. On the front of hiring, how much time do you think founders and leaders should spend on hiring? What percentage of their time have you seen the best founders and leaders spend?
turns.zh: 明白了。所以你亲身经历了这种情况，然后反过来将其转化为优势。我太喜欢了。真是个绝佳的建议。我从未听过这样的见解，听起来真是妙极了。感谢你分享这些心得。谢谢。关于招聘方面，您认为创始人和高管应该花多少时间在这项工作上？您见过最优秀的创始人和高管在这方面投入了多少比例的时间？

turns.speaker: Gokul Rajaram
turns.en: Obviously you've got to always be hiring. Even today, I think Tony and DoorDash, if you have good strong people, you'll always say, "Please make the intro if you have some amazing people," because you never know what you learn from these people, even if you don't end up hiring them. So, always want to meet great people. But I think in general a founder of a young company should spend I think two hours a day hiring and you should do it during the time. I think the challenge in hiring is, you've got to build a process first of all, and that takes a lot of heavy metal work, the right process for you to make sure you do reach out. And again, there are two parts of hiring, there's a lot of reaching out to people and then there's actually talking to people. So I would suggest spending one hour a day doing the reach outs and there it should almost be busy work because you almost figure out the process. (00:39:56): So you should do it during the time of day where you don't have to put a lot of mental... Like, you don't need to be fresh because you need the fresh work for your actual company that you're running. But you need some time, fresh time to come up with the right process. How do you do LinkedIn reach out? Or whatever tools you use to reach out to. Who are the types of profiles, what roles you want to prioritize. So you need to find the right hour to do that in. The second hour should be devoted to actually meeting one or two people on a daily basis, and that's two half an hour conversations. (00:40:26): So I think if you just do that, you'll actually, over even 30 days, think about it, you'll meet with 60 people. And you'll do 30 hours of LinkedIn's, just two hours out of say 10 hours a day. And let's say 20 hours, 20 days. So instead of 30. Because of weekday, that's still a lot of time. So I think two hours. Use Calendar. Calendar is your best friend there, use calendar. And I think that's more than enough to do really well on recruiting.
turns.zh: 显然，你必须始终在招聘上投入精力。即便在今天，我觉得托尼和DoorDash的团队，如果你有优秀的人才，就会不断说：“如果有出色的人选，请帮我们牵线搭桥。”因为你永远不知道能从这些人身上学到什么，即便最终没有聘用他们。所以，要不断结识优秀的人才。但我认为，一般来说，年轻公司的创始人每天应该花两个小时用于招聘，而且应该在这段时间内完成招聘工作。招聘的挑战在于，首先你必须建立一套流程，这需要大量的基础工作，确保你能有效地联系到合适的人才。招聘分为两个部分：一是主动联系潜在候选人，二是与他们实际沟通。所以我建议每天花一小时用于主动联系，这几乎可以算是机械性的工作，因为你会逐渐摸索出合适的流程。（00:39:56）：所以你应该选择一天中不需要耗费大量精力的时间段。比如，你不需要保持头脑清醒，因为你需要把精力投入到实际运营公司的工作中。但你需要一些时间、清醒的时间来制定合适的流程。第二个小时应该用于每天与一到两个人进行面谈，每次对话时长半小时。（00:40:26）：所以我认为，如果你坚持这样做，30天下来，算一算，你就能接触到60个人。每天只需30小时用于LinkedIn招聘，也就是每天两小时。假设每天20小时，持续20天。这样比30天更现实，因为工作日时间更充裕。所以我认为两个小时足够了。使用日历功能。日历是你的好帮手，一定要善加利用。我觉得这足以让你在招聘方面取得出色成果。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I'm guessing that you can see a pretty big difference between the founders that you work with that do this sort of process and put in the time, and don't?
turns.zh: 我猜你能看到，与那些遵循这种流程并投入时间的创始人相比，那些不这样做的创始人会有很大差别吧？

turns.speaker: Gokul Rajaram
turns.en: One hundred percent. I think putting in the process upfront is really important because you can flounder around, and then just spending a few, four, five hours upfront, talking to a few folks, coming with a good process can massively improve the because they say, right, it's all about once you aim the strategy or the direction you're going is much more important than the speed you go in. (00:41:18): If you go in the wrong direction, it doesn't matter how fast you go, you're screwed. But if you go in the right direction, even if you go slightly slower, you're going to get there. So I think it's very important to set the direction of hiring, how exactly are you going to hire, what the process is, what your messaging is going to be, and really make sure you nail that before you do stuff.
turns.zh: 完全正确。我认为提前制定流程非常重要，因为如果你随意摸索，前期花几个小时与几个人交流，制定一个好的流程能极大地提升效率。他们说，没错，制定战略或明确发展方向比速度更重要。（00:41:18）：如果你方向错误，无论速度多快都是徒劳。但如果你方向正确，即便速度稍慢也能达成目标。所以我认为确定招聘方向至关重要：你打算如何招聘，流程是怎样的，宣传语料该如何准备，这些都必须在行动前敲定。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Once you've hired someone, you give them a title. I know you have some strong opinions about titles and how to think about titles at startups and I'd love to hear your take on that.
turns.zh: 招人之后，你会给他们一个头衔。我知道你对初创公司的头衔和职位有自己的看法，很想听听你的见解。

turns.speaker: Gokul Rajaram
turns.en: Yeah, I think on titles, I personally feel that if you're young, you have a unique opportunity as a founder to set a culture in place where people care about scope and impact much more than they would titles. The titles I'm most opposed to, to be honest, I'm not opposed to titles. I think, tweeted about this and people interpret to think no one should have any titles. Titles, people... You want someone to be called a software engineer so you know what they're doing. But the titles I'm most against are director and VP titles. Director, senior director. Because those are the titles that lead to the most contention in the company, that lead to the most conflict, that lead to the most disgruntlement and heartache and managers having to constantly... And people basically staying on for the title, to put it bluntly, versus because their scope and impact. (00:42:39): But I'm also against giving titles too early in a company. For example, I think the general counsel is a good title. I think Wall Street cares about it. It's important to hear who general counsel is, but I was meeting with a 25 person company today and that CEO told me... I was like, I always talk about what keeps you up at night? And this company's in somewhat of a legal heavy space. He is like, "I need to hire a general counsel instantly." I said, "Listen, yes, I know you need to hire a lead lawyer, whatever you call them. Or head of legal, but do not give the general counsel title at a 25 person company because the person at a 250 person company, hopefully you're going to be that in two, three years. It's going to be very different than the GC now. And you might, you still want to retain this person most likely because they're good. (00:43:22): You just don't want them to be the general counsel. She's over and over again. And so, there are certain times you only can give once and if you give it to early, you can't then... That's the reason to avoid title as long as possible. If you give the VP engineering title at 25 people, how the heck are you ever going to have upgrade that person, upgrade that role? You have to basically let them go because you can't then say, "This VP of engineering, now you're going to be made director of engineering or something," et cetera. It's very challenging.
turns.zh: 是啊，我觉得关于头衔的问题，我个人认为，如果你还年轻，作为创始人，你有独特的机会建立一种文化，让人们更关注工作内容和影响力，而不是头衔。说实话，我最反感的头衔不是头衔本身。我在推特上谈过这个话题，人们误解为不应该有任何头衔。头衔嘛，人家希望被称为软件工程师，这样大家都知道他们在做什么。但我最反对的是总监和副总裁之类的头衔。总监、高级总监之类的。因为这些头衔在公司里最容易引发争执、冲突、牢骚，让管理者不断应对各种问题。而人们留在公司更多是为了头衔，而不是因为他们的工作范围和影响力。（00:42:39）但我也反对在公司早期就轻易授予头衔。比如，我觉得总法律顾问是个不错的头衔。华尔街很看重这个职位，每个人都想知道谁是总法律顾问。但今天我和一家25人的公司开会时，那个CEO跟我说……我问，你晚上睡不着觉的时候会想什么？这家公司处于法律事务密集型领域。他说，我现在就需要马上招个总法律顾问。我说，你听着，我知道你需要招个首席律师或者法律总监，但别在25人公司就给人总法律顾问的头衔，因为在250人公司，你可能两三年后才会达到那个级别。现在给人总法律顾问的头衔和两年后就不一样了。你很可能还是想留住这个人，因为他们确实优秀。（00:43:22）但你就是不想让他们当总法律顾问。这种情况下，头衔只能授予一次，如果过早授予，就无法更改了。这就是为什么要尽可能避免早期授予头衔的原因。比如在25人公司授予副总裁工程师头衔，之后你怎么能把他提拔到更高职位呢？你只能放他走，因为你不能说，‘这位副总裁工程师，现在你要升任工程总监之类的’。太难了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: When I look at your LinkedIn, it's always funny because I think you're just like, "Startup helper," or when you were running Caviar, I think it was like, "Someone at Caviar," or something very vague. Clearly you live that yourself.
turns.zh: 看看你的领英主页，总是很有趣。我觉得你一直写着‘初创公司助手’，或者你管理Caviar时，写着‘Caviar的某位成员’之类的，很模糊。

turns.speaker: Gokul Rajaram
turns.en: And I saw the impact of it. I saw at, Square I think was the company, and I think Jack came up with this because he saw that Twitter titles were weaponized in different ways. And so he started this at square and that's where I truly saw the impact and never had a single discussion at Square with my team about what the title should be. And that was amazing. At other companies, always, "I want to be promoted director. I want to be promoted to senior director." It's always, during promotion time. If you ask person what their goal is, even personal goals, sometimes they'll even write, I want to be promoted to director, but never had that. (00:44:37): Had stuff of course around scope, impact, compensation, that's great. I want to have conversation about that, but title? No.
turns.zh: 我亲眼见证了这一影响。我记得在Square公司，我觉得杰克之所以提出这个理念，是因为他注意到Twitter上的职位头衔被各种利用来达到不同目的。于是他在Square公司推行了这一做法，而我正是在那里真正见证了其影响力。在Square，我从未与团队讨论过职位头衔该如何设定。这太棒了。在其他公司，人们总会说：“我想晋升为总监。想晋升为高级总监。”这种情况总是在晋升季才会出现。如果你问某人他们的职业目标是什么——甚至是个人目标——有时他们会写下“我想晋升为总监”，但Square从不如此。（00:44:37）当然，晋升时会考虑职责范围、影响力和薪酬等因素，这很好。但职位头衔呢？完全不考虑。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And just to summarize your advice there, what's kind of the role of thumb of titles if someone hasn't read that post?
turns.zh: 总结一下你的建议，如果有人没读过那篇帖子，职位头衔的作用是什么？

turns.speaker: Gokul Rajaram
turns.en: Delay it as long as possible and try to avoid granting director and VP level titles as long as possible, in particular.
turns.zh: 尽可能拖延，特别是避免过早授予总监和副总裁级别的职位。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Easy. And then delay it, meaning have-
turns.zh: 很简单。然后拖延职位头衔的授予，指的是除软件工程师、产品管理之外的职位？

turns.speaker: Gokul Rajaram
turns.en: Very simple. [inaudible 00:45:05]
turns.zh: 软件工程师、主管。主管或领头人这样的词汇都不错，因为主管清晰地描述了他们的职责，领头人也同样明确他们的工作。比如我的头衔是Caviar主管，然后向我汇报的人员有Caviar产品主管、Caviar工程主管、Caviar战略与运营主管、Caviar销售主管等。职位头衔中的词汇越多，他们的职责就越明确。事实上，你可以看看杰克的新头衔，是Block Head，字面意思不再是高级了。（00:45:40）而是Block Head，我觉得应该更准确地翻译为Block Leader。他是Block的领导者，然后依此类推，层级分明。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And delaying titles, meaning like anything other than just software engineer, product management?
turns.zh: 太棒了。这真是宝贵的建议，感谢你详细解析。在进入激动人心的闪电提问环节之前，我想先谈谈投资方面。你花了大量时间进行天使投资，采用了多种方式。从最初开始到现在，你的投资轨迹是怎样的？

turns.speaker: Gokul Rajaram
turns.en: Software engineer, lead. The word lead, or head of are both good, because the head of very clearly describes what they do or lead also very clearly describes what they do. So my title was Caviar Lead and then the people who reported to me were Caviar product lead, Caviar engineering lead, Caviar strategy and operations lead, Caviar sales lead, et cetera. And so the more words that are in the title, the more focused their role is. In fact, you can look at Jack's new title, it's Block Head, so it's literally not senior anymore. (00:45:40): It's head of block, a block leader I would say probably should be more appropriate. He's a leader block, and then so on, it premieres down.
turns.zh: 我花了很多时间进行天使投资，采用了多种方式。从最初开始到现在，我的投资轨迹是怎样的？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. That's incredibly valuable advice and thank you for getting into the details there. I'd love to transition in to talk about investing a little bit before we get to our exciting lightning round. And so you spent a lot of your time angel investing, investing in a bunch of different ways. What's been your trajectory from just starting to angel invest early on to the scale you're at now?
turns.zh: 太棒了。非常宝贵的建议，感谢你详细解析。在进入激动人心的闪电提问环节之前，我想先谈谈投资方面。你花了大量时间进行天使投资，采用了多种方式。从最初开始到现在，你的投资轨迹是怎样的？

turns.speaker: Gokul Rajaram
turns.en: I started angel investing in 2007, 15 years ago. And like many people, I started because my friends and colleagues were leaving to start companies. This is when I was at Google and they were leaving to start companies. So I literally, without going much, I just wanted to support them because I'd worked with them. And so I just put a small check into their companies and some failed, some did really well. But ultimately I realized that for me, investing is all about supporting people much more so than companies themselves. The company itself, it's about the entrepreneur and the person. So till today, I think I have enjoyed the most and I've really come to believe in myself that I am a founder centric. I believe in the founder much more than I do the market. I think there are market centric investors. [inaudible 00:46:56] is amazing and they are very much believe in a big market. (00:46:59): I strongly believe that great founders, and Airbnb's a great example. They create new markets themselves, or they pivot. I mean, if they realize that a certain market is not good, they'll figure out a way to move. And I'm basically, with my check, the biggest mistakes I made early on were after a few checks I said, "Oh, I'm going to be much more selective. I'm not just going to write checks with all my friends. I'm going to look to see what the market they're in." (00:47:25): So I basically just started making these assumptions, "Oh, well, I should not invest in this company." And turns out, almost all of them were sins of omission. I much more care about sins of omission because you can only lose one X your money. But for me, the relationship with the person, a person I know and respect and good friends with, and I'm not investing in them, I don't want to lose that. (00:47:48): And it's an optionality for me to invest in not just this company, but in every other company they start. Because one of the most interesting patterns I see is, folks who are unsuccessful the first time around, but then use those learnings to start a company in the same or similar space and then succeed. And I'm seeing this more and more happen and I want to have, if you don't invest in their first company, even though you thought they were great because the marketers are great, they won't probably come back to you for the second company either. (00:48:16): So very, very founder centric style of investing, almost like YC, I would say. Closer to YC than anything else because YC invest in just founders at this point, they don't care about the idea. They just care that you're a builder and that you can pivot fast. And if you're a team of builders who can pivot fast, they will invest because they know within three weeks, if you don't have product market fit, they'll get you to pivot three times, and under that excitement, you'll find your product market fit four times. I see this again and again.
turns.zh: 我从2007年开始从事天使投资，至今已有15年了。和许多人一样，我最初投身这项事业，是因为我的朋友和同事们纷纷离职去创办公司。当时我在谷歌工作，而他们正离开谷歌去创业。于是我毫不犹豫地想支持他们，因为我曾与他们共事过。所以我给他们的公司投了小额资金，有些公司失败了，有些则发展得非常好。但最终我意识到，对我而言，投资的核心在于支持人而非公司本身。公司本身固然重要，但关键在于创业者和创始人。直到今天，我最引以为傲的是自己始终以创始人为中心。我比起市场更看重创始人。我相信有些投资者以市场为导向。（00:46:56）这很棒，他们深信大市场。（00:46:59）我坚信优秀的创始人——爱彼迎就是绝佳例证。他们能亲手开创新市场，或是及时调整方向。比如当他们意识到某个市场前景不佳时，就会想办法转型。我早期最大的错误是，投了几笔钱后就自以为高明，说：“我要更有选择性，不能再盲目投资朋友的项目了。我得看看他们的市场前景如何。”（00:47:25）结果发现，这些决定几乎都是因循守旧的错误。我更在意这些错失的机会，因为资金损失可以承受。但对我而言，与创始人建立深厚的信任关系至关重要——我认识并尊敬的优秀人才，若我不投资他们，我会永远失去这样的友谊。（00:47:48）对我而言，投资任何公司都带有高度的选择性，因为我见证过太多初创失败者，通过吸取教训在相同或相似领域成功的案例。我越来越坚信，如果你不投资他们的第一家公司，即便你认为他们的市场洞察力很棒，他们也很难再回头找你投资第二家公司。（00:48:16）所以我的投资风格非常以创始人为中心，几乎和YC如出一辙。比起其他投资机构，YC更偏向于纯粹支持创始人，而非创意本身。他们只看重你的行动力和快速调整的能力。只要你是一个能快速迭代的团队，他们就会投钱，因为他们知道，三周内如果你找不到产品市场匹配点，他们就会让你调整三次。在这种激励机制下，你最终总能找到产品市场匹配点。这点我一次又一次见证过。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that advice and it's the way I think about it too. The only downside is if you have worked at an awesome company or two or three, it becomes a very expensive hobby because you end up knowing a lot of awesome people that are doing great things. So you have to be a little bit careful.
turns.zh: 我很欣赏这种理念，这也正是我思考投资问题的角度。唯一的缺点是，如果你曾在一两家很棒的公司工作过，这会变成一种昂贵的爱好，因为你认识太多正在创造伟业的优秀人才。所以你得保持警惕。

turns.speaker: Gokul Rajaram
turns.en: You've got to really make sure what the motivation. That's what I really want to understand. You don't want folks, there are awesome people, but I do want to make sure they're doing it for the right reason. In other words, they're doing it to solve a problem that they've experienced themselves, or seen. So I really try to get into why they're starting the company and I want to make sure the reason for starting the company is authentic, in that it's a problem that they have observed deeply. (00:49:18): Versus, it's something they read about in Tech Crunch or it's a new US Web three or crypto thing or NFT thing. So I think that's how I suss out. So I don't invest in people, even if they're awesome, when I feel their idea for... The reason they're starting the company is mercenary and they're doing it, because they haven't immersed themselves in the space. Famously, I think the Collison Brothers bought a book, I think on payments, very old book or something I think... Or paper maybe, and read it to fully understand why you want people who really immerse themselves in an industry and live and breathe it before they tackle it.
turns.zh: 你们必须真正确保动机正确。这才是我真正想了解的。我不希望人们只是因为他们很棒就加入，但我确实想确保他们是出于正确的理由才这么做的。换句话说，他们是想解决自己亲身经历过或目睹过的问题。因此，我会深入探究他们创办公司的初衷，并确保这个初衷是真实的，是基于他们对某个问题的深刻观察。（00:49:18）：与之相反，他们可能只是在Tech Crunch上读到某个概念，或者追随美国Web 3.0或加密货币、NFT的潮流。因此，我会通过这些判断。即便对方很出色，我也不会投资于他们的项目，如果我觉得他们的创意动机是逐利的，而他们又没有深入了解过这个领域的话。比如，据说科利森兄弟曾购买了一本关于支付的古老书籍，或许是纸质版的，深入研究才决定投身于某个行业。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Are there other things like that, that you look for? That are just like, "Oh wow, I really need to invest in this."
turns.zh: 还有其他类似的标准吗？那些会让你感叹“哇，我真的需要投资这个项目”。

turns.speaker: Gokul Rajaram
turns.en: The ability to hire talent before even you have... Or ability that, if you can show me that you have this set of amazing people lined up to join you or that you have commitments, or even your founders. I mean, the other thing I look for is definitely two person founding team. At least two is the ideal. I've seen solo founders I'm very nervous about because I think no one person has all the skills you need to start a company. And it's also a lot of things to do. (00:50:18): So I do like to see a really good mix of basically a builder and a seller or a hustler and a hacker, whatever you call them. And I think that two person, I really feel comfortable, however good the one person is, I just feel it's... There are obviously one person founding teams that have worked well, but I think the two or three person founding teams, I feel much. Two is the ideal number. So I look for the two person founding team, complementary skills.
turns.zh: 在创办公司之前就能够招募到人才的能力，或者能够证明你已经组建了优秀团队的能力——无论是创始团队还是核心成员。至少两位创始人是最理想的组合。我曾对独自创业的创始人心存顾虑，因为我认为单靠一个人很难具备创办公司所需的全部技能，而且要处理的事情太多了。（00:50:18）：所以我更倾向于看到一个优秀的团队组合，比如一个建设者和销售者，或者一个实干家和技术高手的组合。无论你怎么称呼他们，我认为两人的团队更让我安心，无论单人创始人有多出色，我都觉得……显然也有成功的单人创始团队，但我认为两到三人的团队更可靠。两人是最理想的组合。因此，我会寻找具有互补技能的两人创始团队。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: These are really, really handy rules of thumb that everybody could use. How do you find time to do this? So you have a full time job, I imagine it's extremely demanding, and then you're also doing a lot of investing for folks that are thinking about doing this on the side. How do you time box this and keep it sustainable and not just to go crazy and burn yourself out?
turns.zh: 这些都是非常实用的经验法则，任何人都可以借鉴。如何找到时间做这些事呢？你有一份全职工作，想必压力极大，还要为那些想兼职创业的人提供投资建议。你是如何合理安排时间、保持可持续性的，避免陷入疯狂或精疲力竭的境地？

turns.speaker: Gokul Rajaram
turns.en: Time boxing. Exactly what you said, Lenny, it's time boxing. Most of the time ironically is spent on DoorDash and... Not ironically. Logically is spent on DoorDash even though it may not appear it. So I spend on DoorDash and what I do is a small percent of my time, I basically... I keep looking at my calendar to see, am I spending more than I've worked, say 10 hours a day? Am I spending more than two to three hours, maximum three, ideally two hours a day on things that are needed to do my work? (00:51:25): And three hours actually is a lot. If you think about half an hour meetings with people, that's six meetings you can do a day, out of 10. And I also do two hours each on both Saturday and Sunday so that I can do four meetings each. So if you think about it, six times five is 30, or four times five is 20, plus another four, plus 4... 28 meetings, that's a lot of meetings you can do with people, et cetera, et cetera. Yeah, so I think it's really time boxing and knowing... I think it is knowing what matters. Because if you find yourself doing the opposite, where 70% of time is investing, then you should actually become a full-time investor.
turns.zh: 时间管理。伦尼，你说得太对了，这就是时间管理。讽刺的是，大多数时间都花在了DoorDash上……不，准确来说，是为了工作而不得不花时间在DoorDash上，尽管表面上看不出来。所以我花在DoorDash上的时间，只占我时间的一小部分。我基本上……我会一直查看日历，确认自己每天工作的时间是否超过了10小时？每天花在工作所需事务上的时间是否超过了两到三小时，理想情况是三小时？（00:51:25）：三小时其实已经很多了。如果你算算和别人开半小时会，一天能开6次会议，总共10次。周六和周日我也会各花两个小时，这样就能分别开四次会议。这样算下来，6次5小时就是30小时，或者4次5小时就是20小时，再加上另外4小时……总共28次会议，能和很多人开会交流，等等等等。是啊，我觉得这就是时间管理，关键在于明白什么才是重要的。因为如果你发现自己在做相反的事情，比如70%的时间都在投资，那你就应该去当全职投资者了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's amazing. I don't know how you keep your brain capacity focused on so many things. Meeting with that many founders, even outside the time, is a lot of mental load.
turns.zh: 太厉害了。我不知道你是怎么能让大脑同时专注于这么多事情的。即使不算时间成本，和这么多创始人见面也需要耗费大量精力。

turns.speaker: Gokul Rajaram
turns.en: I enjoy it. I think the thing is, I enjoy it because I have been a founder myself, not a very successful one. So one of the things I love hearing, I always start with, "Tell me your founding story." And every founder likes to tell the founding story. And that's where I listen closely for authenticity, to understand how they met each other, the two founders or multiple founders, how they knew each other, and how they came up with this idea that they're going after. Versus what problem they're tackling. (00:52:36): I have a standard set of questions I ask so that way I can spend my time not thinking of questions to ask but just listening and just learning. And then I also have a good ability to forget instantly. I take notes and then I just forget and go into the next meeting. So compartmentalizing well.
turns.zh: 我很享受这个过程。我觉得原因在于，我自己也曾是创始人，虽然不是很成功的那种。所以我最喜欢听他们讲创业故事，每次我都会先问：“给我讲讲你的创业故事。”每个创始人都喜欢分享自己的故事。我会仔细聆听他们的真实经历，了解两位或多位创始人是如何相识的，以及他们是如何想出要追逐的那个创意的。而不是他们在解决什么问题（00:52:36）。我有一套标准的问题，这样我就能专注于倾听而不是构思问题。然后我记笔记，记完就忘，接着进入下一场会议。所以善于分隔不同信息。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Have you thought about publishing these questions that you ask? Or do you think that would hurt your chats?
turns.zh: 你有没有想过把这些问题公开发布？还是说你觉得那样会影响交流？

turns.speaker: Gokul Rajaram
turns.en: No, I think it seems... Yeah, it seems too formulaic then. I think there's questions that then change based on what the answer. So it's not exactly a set of questions, but it always starts with, "Tell me about your founding story of the company." I introduce myself and then asked them for their founding story. They're all nervous, pitching, et cetera when they pitch someone who could be an investor. We ask them to tell stories. It's the same for customer interviews, right? You never ask customers, "Tell me your top three problems." (00:53:23): No one knows what they are. But, "Tell me the last time you used a food delivery service. Tell me the last time you used a payment service. How was it? Tell me the last time you took a payment, credit card payment. Tell me about your last customer." People love telling stories about themselves. Everyone likes talking about how they did something.
turns.zh: 不，我觉得那样显得太模式化了。有些问题会根据回答内容而变化。所以这不是固定的一套问题，但总是从“给我讲讲公司的创业故事”开始。我先自我介绍，然后让他们讲创业故事。当他们面对潜在投资者时，都会很紧张，忙着推销项目。我们让他们讲故事。这和客户访谈是一样的，对吧？你永远不会问客户“说说你最头疼的三个问题。”（00:53:23）：没人知道自己的痛点是什么。但“上次你使用外卖服务是什么时候？”“上次你使用支付服务是什么时候？”“体验如何？”“上次你收款（信用卡支付）是什么时候？”“上次你接待的客户是什么样的？”人们喜欢讲述自己的故事。每个人都喜欢谈论自己做过的事。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: For somebody that's thinking about getting into angel investing, other than having capital and finding capital, what advice would you give folks?
turns.zh: 对于那些想涉足天使投资的人来说，除了有资金和寻找资金，还有什么建议吗？

turns.speaker: Gokul Rajaram
turns.en: See, the number one thing you need is, I think, besides... Number one thing is capital. Number zero thing. Number one thing is then you need to have deal flow, as they call it, or companies that you're meeting with and deciding. And then you need to know how to pick these companies. So you need to meet companies, you need to know how pick them. As an angel is generally easy. So I think you need to figure out how to get deal flow. And there are three ways to get deal flow to companies. One, you build your own brand. You can be like Lenny, who's built an incredible brand, or none of us can be like Lenny, but you can try to, we can all publish. The reality is, I used to tell every single person, "You can build your brand on the internet. You can build your brand, social media channels." (00:54:29): There's so many channels. And you have the person here who can teach the masterclass in that. You can build your brand. And just by doing that, you'll get people coming to you. Second, you have a lot of... Anyone in technology has other people they know who are angel investors. So it's just tell them, "Hey, I'd love to help companies. If they're investing in a company, please let we know." And the more people you tell, the more likely it is, they'll remember you. And every time you meet them, reinforce that. And third, investors. If you do know venture capitals or investors, many of them are looking to bring on... There's typically a round when they lead companies around, there's typically an allocation for angels. But for all of those, the first and most important thing is you need to understand, how are you going to add value to these companies? (00:55:13): What is your differentiation? What do you stand for? Why should a company take your money? The best companies have much more than... As Lenny and I both know, their rounds are over subscribed. It is hard enough to get even $1 into their round, let alone a hundred thousand dollars or $5,000. So why would they take your money? And so that's the thing, you have to really figure out. What is your unique differentiation? What do you bring to these companies that no one else can? And I know that's hard, that's painful to figure out, but that is the introspection each of us needs to do. (00:55:44): The way you do that is by just sharing your non-obvious insights. And don't just like... Basically just write. That's why I think writing is so powerful because it shows the world. My rule of thumb is when they do a search for you on Google, if your LinkedIn profile is the first thing that comes up, you've probably done something wrong. (00:56:02): What should come up is an article you wrote. Is a tweet you published. Is someone mentioning you on something else, et cetera. Because that's when, clicking on it, they know what you stand for by that content about you, by you, et cetera. Yes, Mike Morritz can get away with LinkedIn because no one needs to know what he has done. But for the rest of us, we need to build our brand, what we stand for. And it'll change over time. I used to basically believe I should just think about product development, how to lead product teams, engineering teams. For over the last five years, since I've led broader teams, I now share stuff which is much broader than that. And so what I stand for and what value I add has changed and evolved and hopefully increased over time. The same will happen. But you've got to take ownership of your brand on the internet. (00:56:46): No one else can. No one else can. It's not your company. You've got to transcend the companies you work for. If your identity is X, Y, Z, worker drone at A, B, C company, that's not enough. You've got to be X, Y, Z expert in A. Or whatever that A is, even if it's a niche thing, that's okay. Every company leads... So many companies come to me, "I want a payments expert." And then I'll find someone who's a payments expert for them because they're trying to build a fintech practice or something. So be an expert in payments, if that's what you know. Write about non obvious insights on payments. Doesn't need to be a functional discipline like, Lenny and I are doing product or something. Can be a domain. Risk, payments, crypto. Think about crypto, right? The people who got into crypto, and I just read a post by this guy, Richard Chen, he graduated from Stanford. (00:57:33): I don't know him, but I read incredible post. He runs this firm fund called One Confirmation, which is a top fund. He graduated from undergrad four years ago. That's all he did. I mean, he was head of Stanford Blockchain. He wrote, he writes amazing stuff. He's built a brand for himself. Kudos to him. 25 years old, probably. (00:57:50): Never met the guy, but I was like, this guy knows what he's doing. Watch his LinkedIn. Oh my God, he's never worked at a company. He's basically been out of school for four years, but he has incredible insights.
turns.zh:
看，我认为你最需要的首要条件，除了……首要条件就是资金。零号条件。然后你需要有所谓的"交易流"，也就是你接触并评估的公司。接着你得知道如何筛选这些公司。作为天使投资人，通常这并不难。所以关键在于如何获取交易流。获取交易流有三种途径：第一，打造个人品牌。比如莱尼（Lenny）就成功打造了个人品牌——虽然我们没法像他那样，但至少可以尝试发布内容。现实中我常告诉大家："你可以在互联网上建立个人品牌，通过社交媒体渠道推广。"（00:54:29）：渠道实在太多了。在座就有能讲授这方面大师课的人。只要持续努力，自然会有人主动找上门。第二，拓展人脉。科技领域从业者往往认识很多天使投资人。直接告诉他们："我很乐意帮助创业公司。若他们有投资需求，请告知我。"多多宣传，总有机会被记住。每次见面时都要强化这个印象。第三，利用投资人资源。若你认识风投或其他投资者，他们通常会为天使投资人预留份额。但最关键的是，你要明白如何为这些公司创造价值？你的独特价值主张是什么？为什么公司要选择你？最成功的公司远不止这些。莱尼和我都知道，他们的融资轮次往往超额认购。即便融到1美元都困难，更别说10万或5万美元了。所以为什么要选择你？这就需要深思熟虑：你的独特价值在哪里？你能为公司带来别人无法复制的资源？这确实很痛苦，但这正是我们每个人需要自省的。（00:55:44）：方法就是分享你非显性的洞察。别只顾自己埋头苦干。写作就是强大的工具，因为它能向世界展示你的价值。我的经验法则是：当别人在谷歌搜索你时，如果首页出现的是领英资料，那你可能做错了。应该出现的是你写的文章、发布的推文、他人提及你的内容等。这时点击链接，人们就能通过这些内容了解你的主张和价值。迈克·莫里茨（Mike Morritz）可以靠领英混，因为没人需要了解他的过往。但对我们其他人来说，必须打造个人品牌，明确自己的主张。随着时间推移，我的观点也发生了变化。过去五年，我专注于产品开发、团队管理。但现在我领导更广泛的团队后，分享的内容也更加多元化。我的核心价值观和贡献也随之升级。未来还会有更多改变。但你必须掌控自己在互联网上的品牌形象。（00:56:46）：没人能替代你。这不是你的公司。这是你的个人品牌。
听着，如果你的身份是X、Y、Z，或者A、B、C公司的普通员工，那还远远不够。你得成为A领域的X、Y、Z专家。无论A代表的是什么行业，哪怕是小众领域，也没关系。每个公司都在引领行业……很多公司来找我说：“我们需要支付领域的专家。”然后我会为他们找到合适的人选，因为他们正试图拓展金融科技业务之类的。所以，如果你精通支付领域，那就专注于支付领域的深度洞察。无需局限于某个职能领域，比如我和Lenny专注于产品开发之类的。你可以选择某个垂直领域，比如风险管理、支付、加密货币。想想加密货币领域吧，那些涉足加密货币的人——我刚读了Richard Chen的帖子，他毕业于斯坦福大学。（00:57:33）我不认识他，但他的帖子写得太棒了。他经营着顶级基金One Confirmation，四年前才本科毕业。这就是他全部的经历。他曾担任斯坦福区块链俱乐部的主席，写作水平一流，成功打造了个人品牌。真为他点赞。他大概25岁吧。（00:57:50）虽然没见过他，但我觉得这家伙很专业。看看他的领英主页，天啊，他从未在公司工作过。四年前毕业后，他就专注于研究，积累了深刻的见解。

turns.zh: 等他听到这期播客就知道了。他肯定会说：“天哪，他们在谈论我呢。”

turns.speaker: Gokul Rajaram
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是啊。

Whatever comes to mind, let me know. If nothing comes to mind, that's also cool. And then we will wrap up. Are you ready?
turns.zh: 我希望他是听众，如果不是的话，我们得找到他。好的，现在进入闪电问答环节。我要快速问大家几个问题，想到什么就说什么。如果想不出来，那也没关系。然后我们就结束。准备好了吗？

turns.en: Perfect. Ready.
turns.zh: 完美。准备好了。

turns.zh: 好的。你推荐给其他产品负责人的书最多的是哪本？

turns.speaker: Gokul Rajaram
turns.en: Playing to Win: How Strategy Really Works. It's a book called Playing to Win and the subtitle is How Strategy Really Works. Very good book.
turns.zh: 《玩转战略：战略如何真正奏效》。这本书叫《Playing to Win》，副标题是《战略如何真正奏效》。非常棒的一本书。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. I have not read that. I will check that out. What's a company that you recommend to people that are looking for new gigs? Maybe product managers, maybe any other function?
turns.zh: 太棒了。我还没读过。我会去看看的。你推荐给正在寻找新工作的产品经理或其他职位的人的公司是哪家？

turns.speaker: Gokul Rajaram
turns.en: DoorDash. Incredible operational excellence. And what you learn here, I have myself learned a lot in the two years I've been here, about new ways of the attention to detail. Operational excellence, unparalleled.
turns.zh: DoorDash。运营卓越得令人惊叹。在这里学到的东西，我自己在这两年里也收获颇丰，特别是对细节的关注。运营卓越，堪称无与伦比。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I usually include, you can't mention the company you're working at now. Is there another company by any chance? And if not, you can have that.
turns.zh: 通常不允许提及你现在工作的公司。不过你要是方便的话，可以说说其他公司。既然不方便，那就不提了。

turns.speaker: Gokul Rajaram
turns.en: I would say Coinbase, if you're interested in crypto. I am technically a board member. I truly believe. I think if you are interested in crypto, Coinbase has such a diverse set of things that they work on that it is literally, you can work on almost any part of crypto, from NFTs to wallets to custody to infrastructure. They have a company they called Bison Trails, which does infrastructure. So you can truly, it's like Google, worked on everything. You could work in YouTube, you can work in search. Coinbase, I think the same thing. You can work in 10 different products and within two years or three years, learn the complete spectrum, crypto ecosystem.
turns.zh: 如果对加密货币感兴趣的话，我会推荐Coinbase。我在技术上是董事会成员。我深信不疑。如果你对加密货币感兴趣，Coinbase涉及的领域非常广泛，从NFT、钱包、托管到基础设施。他们还有一家叫Bison Trails的公司，专门做基础设施。所以你真的可以像谷歌那样，接触到各个领域。你可以参与YouTube、搜索等业务。Coinbase也是如此。你可以在10个不同的产品中工作，两三年内就能了解整个加密货币生态系统。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Also an Airbnb alumni founder.
turns.zh: 他还是Airbnb的创始人之一。

turns.speaker: Gokul Rajaram
turns.en: That's right.
turns.zh: 没错。

turns.en: What's your favorite app right now?
turns.zh: 你现在最喜欢的应用是什么？

turns.speaker: Gokul Rajaram
turns.en: Over the last few weeks it has been Coinbase wallet. I've been playing around. I just was a hoarder. I basically just had held Bitcoin Ether for many, many years, but then over the last couple of months I just said, got to just... In the Coinbase board meetings, you listen to all of these things. I'm like... Got to now diverse and beyond and actually got to start staking stuff, going on distributed exchanges, or decentralized exchanges and just basically playing around with Coinbase wallet because earlier I wasn't using wallet. I was just using Coinbase dot com where you can't do any of this stuff. And then DoorDash is the other one. I think I truly use it to order food every day. But Coinbase wallet is one I'm using a lot now.
turns.zh: 过去几周我一直在用Coinbase钱包。我一直在试玩。我之前是个囤积者。我基本上把比特币和以太币囤了好多年，但最近几个月我意识到，必须得多元化发展，真正开始参与质押、分布式交易所之类的活动。所以我现在经常用Coinbase钱包，因为之前我没用过钱包功能，只能用Coinbase官网，而那里根本没这些功能。DoorDash是另一个我常用的。我觉得自己现在每天都在用它点餐。但Coinbase钱包是我现在用得最多的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. I got to check that out. I just got access to the Coinbase NFT stuff, and so yes, it'll pull me into the Coinbase ecosystem. Okay, a couple more questions. Who is a favorite person to follow on Twitter or Instagram? Especially these days?
turns.zh: 太棒了。我得去看看。我刚获得了Coinbase NFT的访问权限，所以这肯定会让我深入Coinbase生态系统。好的，再问几个问题。你最喜欢在Twitter或Instagram上关注的人是谁？尤其是最近这段时间？

turns.en: Exactly. [inaudible 01:00:40].
turns.zh: 确实如此。[01:00:40的背景音]。

turns.zh: 简单选择。好的。这些年来，你遇到过的最喜欢的经理是谁？

turns.speaker: Gokul Rajaram
turns.en: All of them. I've learned different things through them. So no easy choice there.
turns.zh: 他们都是。我从他们身上学到了不同的东西。所以没法轻易选出最喜欢的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: No favorites. All right. Taking the easy way out. And then what's a favorite interview question that you like to ask in interviews? Not with founders, but with hiring.
turns.zh: 没有最喜欢的。好吧。偷懒一下。那么，你在面试中最喜欢问的一个问题是什么？不是针对创始人，而是针对招聘时的问题。

turns.speaker: Gokul Rajaram
turns.en: What are you most proud of? The interview question is a good one. Tell me about something that you're most proud of. What is the accomplishment, career accomplishment you're most proud of? Because it tells you how they measure their impact. Tells you a lot about what they care about, how they measure their impact. If they say, "As a PM I launched X, Y, Z feature," they're talking about the impact and the kind they value it. Something about that. Or if they talk too much about them versus the team, et cetera. So you get a lot from that question. It's a loaded question.
turns.zh: 你最引以为傲的是什么？这个面试问题很棒。请告诉我你最引以为傲的事情。什么是你最自豪的职业成就？因为这能让你了解他们如何衡量自己的影响力。能让你深入了解他们所关注的重点，以及他们如何衡量自己的影响力。如果他们说：“作为产品经理，我推出了X、Y、Z功能，”那他们就是在谈论影响力以及他们所看重的东西。如果他们过多地谈论自己而非团队等等，那么你能从这个问题中获得很多信息。这是个很有深意的问题。

turns.zh: 我在Twitter上，账号是GokulR。还有，我总是说帮助我最好的方式，就是帮助整个生态系统。传递善意，如果你传递善意，最终你帮助的人也会反过来帮助我。但如果我们所有人都传递善意，世界会变得更美好。传递善意吧。然后，就像我一开始说的，要相信机缘巧合的力量，我需要去听听Lenny的TED演讲讲这个话题。

turns.en: Amazing. What a great way to wrap it up. Thank you so much for being here. Gokul.
turns.zh: 太棒了。真是个完美的收尾。非常感谢你今天的到来。Gokul。

turns.en: Thank you, Lenny. Thanks for having me.
